source_read: PubMed Central full text PMC3053129, read in my own browser tab (tab-7, which I opened and closed; no other tab touched, nothing downloaded): abstract, all sections, Tables 1-4 as text, Figure 1 legend, acknowledgments and footnotes, and reference entries 61 and 62. Step 1 (blind extraction) not run this round, per the round brief.

design.note: Cross-sectional comparison of two groups from the same dance scene, with biological screening for undisclosed drug use; the card says what it can and cannot establish.

key_findings.note: Checked PMC Results, 1st paragraph; all five numbers and the six relaxed cases match.
Checked Table 1 and Results, 2nd paragraph: median 43.5 (27, 87.3); 121 days (60, 209); shortest 25 days, 3 (6%) under 40; 22 heavy and 30 moderate.
Checked Table 1: all five comparisons and their p values match.

Checked Table 2: all five rows match. The differences are non-users minus users, per the table's footnote, so the CVLT estimate of -0.5 means the ecstasy group scored slightly higher after adjustment.
Checked Table 2: all seven entries match, including the two at p = 0.05 and verbal IQ at p = 0.06.

Checked Table 3, heavy-user columns, and Results, 2nd paragraph. I also scanned that column for any other p < 0.05 and found none (nearest: spatial span total and backward, p = 0.09), so 'no other differences' holds.

Checked Table 3, moderate-user columns: Raven's p = 0.02, digit symbol p = 0.02, vocabulary p = 0.03, Wisconsin categories p = 0.03, spatial span forward p = 0.04, i.e. the stated range; the text's 'only among moderate users' sentence is in Results, 2nd paragraph.
Checked Results, 2nd paragraph and the Figure 1 legend; coefficient, interval, p value and r all match.

Checked Results, 3rd paragraph and Table 4. The 14 values run 0.37 to 0.76, so a large effect (0.8) is excluded on all 14. The editors' count of 6 for a medium effect is right if the column is read as the effect that can be rejected (values at or below 0.50: 0.37, 0.40, 0.48, 0.49, 0.49, 0.50); a strict reading of 'below 0.5' gives 5, because the Iowa Gambling Task sits exactly at 0.50. Either way the authors' 'many' covers fewer than half the measures.
Checked Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; each element is there, including the authors' own caution that cross-sectional data cannot show impulsivity to be caused by ecstasy.
Checked Discussion, 3rd paragraph: 59.5 vs 121 days, unmeasured confounders, chance.

Checked Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs: the false-negative reading with 6 participants at 150 or more episodes, the opposite reading, and the closing sentence that the question remains incompletely resolved.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed against Table 4 (see key finding 8): a medium effect is excluded on 6 of 14 measures at best, and the eight remaining values run 0.53 to 0.76.

Confirmed: 'Exploratory analyses suggest' is the whole basis given for setting the pegboard difference aside, and the two robustness checks (simplified model; exclusion of the 6 relaxed cases) are reported only as yielding very similar results.
Confirmed: 88.5 (8.8) in Table 2 and 88.5 (8.7) in Table 3 for the same 59 people.
Confirmed: both tables are titled 'Representative Neuropsychological Test Scores', and nothing states whether all scored variables appear.

instrument.note: ROBINS-E, correct for a non-randomized study of an exposure.

domains.note: Some concerns is right: the adjustment set is unusually full (family of origin, childhood conduct disorder, ADHD) but marijuana intoxications and all-night parties still differ and are not in it.
Breath, urine and hair testing is the strongest exposure verification in this batch; lifetime episodes remain self-reported.
About 111 of 1500 screened; the card is right that this is a deliberately unusual sample, which is the study's design, not a flaw, but it limits who the result describes.
Blinding of the tester is indeed not reported anywhere in the paper.
'Representative' tables, about 40 measures without correction by stated choice, and equivalence bounds for 14 chosen measures only.

overall.note: Some concerns, matching the worst domain; the reasoning's restriction (citable for small or absent differences after moderate use with minimal other drug use, and for the exclusion of large differences) is what the paper supports.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right. The abstract states the negative finding with its caveat, the Discussion gives both readings and the authors do not claim to have shown safety. The one strain is 'we could exclude even a medium effect on many cognitive measures', which Table 4 supports for 6 of 14.

missed: The measures on which a medium effect could not be excluded cluster in working memory and visuospatial span (spatial span total 0.76, digits backwards 0.69, digit symbol 0.66, block design 0.64), which is the domain in which Murphy et al. (2009) report the most consistent differences. The card treats Table 4 as a single statement about precision; this pattern is what a reader comparing the two sources will want, and it limits the null to verbal memory much more than to span tasks.

The authors' own 2004 pilot, with the same design and a smaller sample, found differences in heavier use that this larger study did not reproduce (Introduction, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph). The card records this under replication, but the key findings do not say that this paper is a failed self-replication, which is the single most important fact about it for the contested claim.

Discussion, 4th paragraph describes Schilt et al. (2007) (reference 61) and Gouzoulis-Mayfrank et al. (2005) (reference 62); I checked both reference entries, so the card's attribution of the 38-person, 18-month study to Gouzoulis-Mayfrank is correct and can be recorded as verified rather than inferred.
Funding and conflicts check out against the article: NIDA grant DA017953 in the acknowledgments and a footnote stating no conflicts and no tobacco, alcohol, pharmaceutical or gaming industry support.
